witness_description: V = {0,1,2}; tree T with edges {(0,1),(0,2)}; S = {0}, V\S = {1,2}; e1 = (0,1), which has one endpoint in S and one in V\S ('e1 connects these two sets'). Removing e1 from T yields exactly two components, {0,2} and {1} - not S = {0} and V\S = {1,2}.
refutation_explanation: The claim's first part (a tree edge is a bridge whose removal leaves exactly two components) holds, but the second part asserts that those two components 'must be precisely S and V\S' merely because e1 connects S to V\S. That inference is false whenever more than one tree edge crosses the cut (S, V\S). In the witness, both tree edges (0,1) and (0,2) cross the cut; removing the crossing edge e1 = (0,1) gives components {0,2} and {1}, neither of which equals S or V\S. The components equal S and V\S only if e1 is the UNIQUE tree edge crossing the cut, a hypothesis the quoted text does not state.
search_space: All labeled trees T on V = {0,...,n-1} for n = 2..5 (every (n-1)-subset of the C(n,2) edges forming a connected acyclic graph, edges in lexicographic order), all nonempty proper subsets S of V (by increasing bitmask), and every tree edge e1 with exactly one endpoint in S (lexicographic order). For each triple, exact integer/set computation of the components of T - e1, checking (a) exactly two components and (b) components == {S, V\S}. Deterministic fixed iteration order; first violation reported (found at n=3).
